newsitem.title: UK: FX in Europe: Dollar stands tall, stg shrivels.
newsitem.headline: FX in Europe: Dollar stands tall, stg shrivels.

text.p: The dollar zoomed to a fresh near-eight year high against the mark for the fourth consecutive trading day amid further signs that the German government and the Bundesbank will not act to support the battered mark.
A setback of over a pfennig from its highs in late trade here was a necessary consolidation for a move up to psychological resistance at 1.90 marks, traders said.

The dollar failed to hold on to overnight gains against the yen though amid concern that a rise above 120 will increase trade friction and attract central bank intervention. Dollar/yen hit a 12-week high at 119.58 overnight, buoyed by expectations that Japanese interest rates will remain low to support the ailing economy.

"Dollar/mark is boosted by the market's view that the Bundesbank won't dare to raise rates, but dollar/yen is undermined by concern that the 120 level will not be tolerated as it would cause trade friction," said Francis Breedon, currency strategist at Lehman Brothers. Sterling suffered at the hands of the strong dollar. The pound fell to its lowest level in nearly five months below $1.60 as doubts emerged whether the Bank of England would raise interest rates on Thursday. Sterling/mark tumbled along with cable, shedding four pfennigs and testing waters around 3.0 marks.

Traders had speculated the Bundesbank could prepare the ground for higher money-market rates by keeping the market short of liquidity at its money-market transactions on Wednesday. Mark selling gathered pace after such talk proved to be unfounded when the central bank provided the market with a generous injection of funds.
Comments from a German government spokesman about recent forex developments were also seen as supporting the dollar rally, traders said.

The spokesman said the dollar's rise was due to "speculative effects" ahead of European economic and monetary union and that from a German perspective there was no reason to "dramatise" recent developments in the foreign exchange markets.
The dollar was also boosted against the mark after a German jobless report fanned expectations that the economic recovery is too fragile to allow the Bundesbank to raise rates too far.

The dollar rose as high as 1.8913 marks, the strongest it has been since October 1989. It was at 1.8786/96 at 1440 GMT from 1.8788/92 late Tuesday in Europe. Dollar/yen was at 119.05/15, off its overnight peak at 119.58 and little changed from 119.01/11 yesterday.
The Bundesbank has encouraged speculation that it will engineer higher money-market rates if mark weakness persists.
This has failed to deter dollar bulls, though, who expect the Bundesbank cannot raise its securities repurchase rate high enough in the face of economic fragility to stave off mark selling.

They got encouragement from a report today which showed the number of jobless in Germany rose by a seasonally adjusted 17,000 in July and that the unadjusted jobless rate rose to 11.4 percent from 11.0 percent in June.
"The Bundesbank's barrels are empty in terms of what they can do to defend the currency," said Paul Lambert, senior currency strategist at UBS Ltd in London.
"The trend is very much consistent with the economic fundamentals, as the jobless numbers showed, and if they try to raise rates it will be negative for the economy."
With the earliest likely opportunity for the Bundesbank to switch to variable-rate repos now next week, traders are gunning for a move above 1.90 marks in the coming days.

Expectations that Japanese interest rates will stay at record lows were reinforced after Japanese Vice Finance Minister Takeshi Komura said overnight that the low interest-rate policy the Bank of Japan was following still had positive economic effects.
His comments overshadowed remarks made by a U.S. embassy official in Tokyo about the potential for trade friction between the U.S. and Japan and buoyed dollar/yen.
Lawrence Greenwood, the economic minister-counsellor at the U.S. embassy said that the increases in Japan's current account could trigger trade tensions between the two countries.
